theory.intro: A **prime** number has exactly two factors: $1$ and itself. A **composite** number has more than two factors.
facts: $1$ is **neither** prime nor composite; $2$ is the only even prime.
steps: Count the factors of the number.
Exactly two factors → prime; more than two → composite.
$1$ has only one factor, so it is neither.

foundation.question_text: Classify $13$ as prime, composite or neither.
foundation.solution_text:
The factors of $13$ are $1$ and $13$.
It has exactly two factors, so $13$ is prime.

foundation.question_text: Classify $15$ as prime, composite or neither.
foundation.solution_text:
The factors of $15$ are $1,3,5,15$.
It has more than two factors, so $15$ is composite.

The factors of $2$ are $1$ and $2$.
It has exactly two factors, so $2$ is prime.

foundation.question_text: Classify $1$ as prime, composite or neither.
foundation.solution_text: $1$ has only one factor, so it is neither prime nor composite.

foundation.question_text: Classify $0$ as prime, composite or neither.
foundation.solution_text: $0$ is not a positive integer, so it is neither prime nor composite.

foundation.question_text: Classify $21$ as prime, composite or neither.
foundation.solution_text:
$3 \times 7=21$
So $21$ has factors other than $1$ and itself and is composite.

development.solution_text:
$33=3 \times 11$, $39=3 \times 13$ and $51=3 \times 17$.
Only $37$ has exactly two factors, so $37$ is prime.
$49=7 \times 7$, so $49$ has more than two factors and is composite.

development.question_text:
A number has factors $1,5,7,35$.
Classify it.
development.solution_text: The number has four factors, so it is composite.

development.question_text:
A student says every even number is composite.
Use $2$ to correct the claim.
development.solution_text:
$2$ has exactly two factors, $1$ and $2$.
Therefore $2$ is prime, so not every even number is composite.

development.question_text: Classify $81$ as prime, composite or neither and give a factor pair as evidence.
development.solution_text:
$9 \times 9=81$
So $81$ has more than two factors and is composite.

development.question_text:
A number has exactly two distinct factors.
What classification must it have?
development.solution_text: A positive integer with exactly two distinct factors is prime.

mastery.question_text:
A student says $1$ is prime because it can only be divided by $1$.
Explain the error.
mastery.solution_text: A prime number needs exactly two distinct factors. $1$ has only one distinct factor, so it is neither prime nor composite.

mastery.question_text: Without listing every factor, decide whether $91$ is prime or composite.
mastery.solution_text:
$7 \times 13=91$
So $91$ has factors other than $1$ and itself and is composite.

mastery.question_text:
A positive integer has the factor pair $11 \times 11$.
Can it be prime?
Explain.
mastery.solution_text: No. It has $1$, $11$ and the number itself as distinct factors, so it is composite.
